newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Tapes show Colombia Cali kingpins not most powerful.
newsitem.headline: Tapes show Colombia Cali kingpins not most powerful.

text.p: Leaders of the once-mighty Cali drug cartel were not only hunted by the Colombian authorities but also came under fire from gangsters even more powerful and ruthless than themselves, according to secret recordings published on Sunday.

Excerpts from the conversation said to have taken place in May between the cartel's No. 2, Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela, in Bogota's La Picota prison, the No. 3, Pablo "Pacho" Herrera, who was still on the run, also indicate that the jailed drug lord maintained some control of trafficking operations even behind bars -- a claim frequently made by the U.S. authorities.

In an article on Sunday, leading daily El Tiempo said the recordings were made by police intelligence the day after Rodriguez Orejuela's son William survived an attack in a Cali restaurant, in which two of his bodyguards and four lunch partners died.

In the conversation, a frightened Herrera, who surrended to police on Sept. 1, told Rodriguez Orejuela: "I don't know what to do. You haven't got a single ally. We haven't got anybody, even the ones we called friends are the ones causing us most harm."

Years before, in the early 1990s, heads of the Cali cartel successfully plotted the downfall of the formerly unrivaled drug baron Pablo Escobar and his Medellin cartel with direct attacks, and by passing on information to the security forces, according to drug experts.

Until Sunday's publication of the tapes, the credit for largely dismantling the Cali cartel -- with the capture of Rodriguez Orejuela and his brother Gilberto last year -- had gone to the police's elite anti-drug squad.
But the tape recordings show that the Cali cartel was, like that of Medellin, under fire from two sides, at the hands of the security forces and from rival gangsters within the drugs underworld.
Herrera and Rodriguez Orejuela referred to a man they call "El senor del Overol", literally the "man with the overalls," whom they said ordered the attack on William Rodriguez.

Herrera said the man was worse than the late drug lord Escobar, notorious for attacks against his rivals and the state, and said there was no way they could fight against him. They did not give any other indication who the man was nor where he was from.

Additionally, the excerpts hint that Herrera may not just have handed himself over to the authorities to plea bargain and get a substantial reduction in his eventual sentence, but also because he, like other drug barons before him, may have felt more vulnerable outside than in a secure prison, out of reach of his rivals.
